title: Kali Uchis Launches For the Girls Tour with Cinematic Flair, Reveals Finished Spanglish Album
summary: Kali Uchis knows how to make an entrance. At Chicago's Grant Park on Saturday, the Colombian-American star arrived onstage in a carriage — a deliberate homage to Selena's iconic 1995 Astrodome performance — and launched her For the Girls tour with a set that was equal parts cinematic spectacle and intimate empowerment. Dressed in a custom all-white, western-inspired ensemble, Uchis glided through nearly an hour of hits, her velvety vocals floating over the festival crowd. The performance was meticulously crafted: sleek choreography with mirror-heavy tableaux, sensual chair routines with male dancers, and a theatricality that has become her signature. Fan favorites like "Telepatía," "After the Storm," and "Moonlight" felt fresh in this evolved production. In an exclusive interview with Billboard Español before the show, Uchis revealed she has a whole album finished. "It's in Spanglish," she said, hinting at a bilingual project that reflects her dual identity. She also explained why Mariah the Scientist was the perfect tour partner: "I love her songwriting. I think she's an amazing, really talented girl and this tour is for the girls!" Uchis emphasized her goal for the tour: "I want them to feel inspired, empowered, to feel a sense of community." She spoke candidly about coming from nothing and lacking family support, using her story to champion self-belief. "I was never gonna believe the things that outwardly people wanted me to believe about myself. It was always very important for me for my inner voice to be the loudest voice." The For the Girls Tour continues with stops in New York, Atlanta, and Los Angeles. With a finished album in the wings, Uchis is clearly in a creative peak, balancing vulnerability and strength in a show designed to lift up her audience.
why_it_matters: Kali Uchis's story shows how an artist's identity—cultural, linguistic, and personal—can become a superpower in the music industry. For a middle schooler, it demonstrates that embracing where you come from and staying true to your inner voice can shape not just a career, but a movement that lifts others up.

background_read: Selena Quintanilla, the 'Queen of Tejano Music,' performed at the Houston Astrodome in 1995 in what became one of her last—and most legendary—shows before her tragic death later that year; her glamorous looks and carriage entrance remain iconic.
Kali Uchis, born in Virginia to Colombian parents, won a Grammy for her album *Red Moon in Venus* and is known for blending R&B, soul, and Latin pop with both English and Spanish lyrics.
Grant Park in Chicago is a huge public park that hosts major music festivals such as Lollapalooza, as well as large-scale concerts and cultural events.
Mariah the Scientist is an American singer-songwriter whose genre-blurring work mixes R&B, pop, and trap; she has gained a cult following for her candid storytelling.

The term 'Spanglish' reflects the lived experience of many bilingual communities in the U.S., where switching between Spanish and English is natural—artists increasingly release albums in Spanglish to capture their dual identity authentically.

perspectives.description: Fans get an immersive, theatrical concert that celebrates female camaraderie and cultural heritage. The announcement of a finished Spanglish album excites listeners who see themselves in bilingual art, and the tour's 'for the girls' theme promotes solidarity.

Some might view the elaborate stagecraft as a distraction from raw vocal talent; overproduction can overshadow musical substance. Additionally, regional tours may exclude international fans who feel left out of the empowering experience.

Uchis's homage to Selena Quintanilla and her embrace of Spanglish are part of a longstanding tradition in Latin music of honoring predecessors while pushing bilingual boundaries. The success of such tours illustrates how American pop is becoming increasingly multiethnic.

If the Spanglish album performs well, it could encourage major labels to invest more in artists who refuse to stick to one language, reshaping the mainstream. The tour's focus on empowerment may also inspire more artist-led movements that prioritize community over commercial spectacle.
